book: 308 - The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy

chapters.file: ch17 - 15. Grey’s Anatomy as Philosophy Ethical Ambiguity in Shades of Grey.md
chapters.relation: The chapter argues that Meredith Grey embodies Simone de Beauvoir's existentialist ethics from The Ethics of Ambiguity, rejecting the childlike 'spirit of seriousness' that treats moral rules as absolute. Through episodes where Meredith stabilizes a bomb inside a patient's chest, coaches a death-row inmate to induce his own brain death, switches an Alzheimer's-trial placebo for Adele, and commits insurance fraud to treat an immigrant child, it shows her breaking institutional protocol to positively will the freedom of others while owning her choices. It contrasts her authentic embrace of moral ambiguity and risk against Shepherd's, Bailey's, and Webber's rule-bound seriousness or self-interest, framing medical dilemmas as an ambiguous moral realm where no single correct answer exists.

chapters.file: ch18 - 16. House of Cards as Philosophy Democracy on Trial.md
chapters.relation: The chapter uses the Underwoods' extra-electoral rise to autocracy in House of Cards to test Plato's and Hobbes's antidemocratic arguments. Frank and Claire exploit the exact weaknesses Plato's Republic diagnoses—Thrasymachus's 'justice is the advantage of the stronger,' the decay of oligarchy into freedom-loving democracy into tyranny, and Peter Russo as the disordered-soul 'democratic man' and 'drone.' It then invokes Hobbes's Leviathan, arguing the show's power-struggle resembles a state of nature and that Hobbes would welcome Claire's absolute rule as more predictable and less corrupt than democracy, before weighing modern defenses of democracy (Levitsky and Ziblatt, Locke, Mill, Rawls, Sen) against these critiques.

chapters.file: ch19 - 17. Last Week Tonight as Philosophy The Importance of Jokalism.md
chapters.relation: The chapter coins 'jokalism' to categorize Last Week Tonight with John Oliver as a new satire paradigm that fuses investigative journalism, fact-checking, and calls to action with comedy. It grounds this in the philosophy of humor—Plato's and Aristotle's suspicion of laughter and the 'superiority theory' running through Hobbes, Freud, and Bergson—and links satire to moral philosophy via the gap between ideal and actual politics. Using Oliver's segments on net neutrality, the death penalty, and the Equal Rights Amendment, it shows how the show builds a philosophical argument (problem, ideal, remedy) that provokes real-world change like the FCC website crash, arguing jokalism boosts critical thinking rather than mere infotainment.

chapters.file: ch20 - 18. Russian Doll as Philosophy Life Is Like a Box of Timelines.md
chapters.relation: The chapter treats Russian Doll's time loops (Season One) and time portals (Season Two) as vehicles for the metaphysics of time, comparing them to Groundhog Day and canvassing presentism, eternalism, and the growing-block theory. It argues the show is committed to a Parfit-style 'multiple timelines' solution to the problem of whether looped characters are numerically identical, and rejects a Berkeleyan idealist alternative. Its climax reads Nadia through Camus's Myth of Sisyphus: unable to change significant past events, she becomes an 'absurd hero' who embraces her family and lot in life, smiling in the mirror, so Season Two's lesson (echoing Nietzsche's eternal recurrence) is that meaning comes from owning one's circumstances.

chapters.file: ch21 - 19. The Orville as Philosophy The Dangers of Religion.md
chapters.relation: The chapter argues that Seth MacFarlane's The Orville is a pointed critique of religion, especially when merged with political and military power. Through the warrior-god Avis worshipped by the Krill (read as stand-ins for militant evangelicals and Islamist jihadists) and the Moclans' patriarchal bigotry, it contends religion is portrayed as archaic and dangerous. It deploys Socrates's Euthyphro argument to reject divine command theory, contrasts the Krill's dogmatic certainty with the secular Union's self-correcting ethics, and invokes Buber's I–Thou to explain the 'de-souling' of outsiders, while defending Lockean separation of church and state against theocracy and theonomistic ethics.

chapters.file: ch22 - 20. Westworld as Philosophy A Commentary on Colonialism.md
chapters.relation: The chapter reads all three seasons of Westworld as a commentary on colonialism, mapping the Delos parks onto settler, planter (extractive labor), and postcolonial colonialism and treating the android hosts as a metaphor for colonized and enslaved peoples. Using Fanon's Wretched of the Earth and Kelly Oliver's colonization of psychic space, it analyzes the hosts' double alienation and the colonizer's dehumanizing projections; it applies Charles Mills's Racial Contract and 'epistemology of ignorance' (with Locke's labor-property justification for dispossession) to the parks' two-tiered order. It casts William/the Man in Black as Memmi's 'colonizer who refuses' turned 'colonizer who accepts,' and Serac's Rehoboam as surveillance-capitalist coloniality, ending on Dolores and Caleb's cross-race solidarity as the hard path to real freedom.

chapters.file: ch23 - 21. Black Mirror as Philosophy A Dark Reflection of Human Nature.md
chapters.relation: The chapter asks whether Black Mirror condemns technology or human nature, and argues for the latter: the 'black mirror' reflects the viewer's character. It tests and rejects the reading of the show as depicting Bostrom-style existential risk or superintelligence (via 'Metalhead' and 'San Junipero') and rejects that Clark and Chalmers's extended-mind coupling (the 'grain' in 'The Entire History of You,' 'Arkangel,' 'Crocodile') destroys human identity. Drawing on Frankfurt School critique—Adorno and Horkheimer's culture industry, Marcuse's one-dimensional man—and Plato's and Aristotle's natural-versus-artificial distinction, it concludes technology is an agency-less imitation that magnifies preexisting human vices, and closes with Benjamin's reproducibility thesis and Bandersnatch's interactivity to suggest the show can prompt viewers to confront their own darkness.

holes.name: Colonialism / Coloniality
holes.what: The theory and practice of domination in which a foreign minority rules, exploits, and dehumanizes an indigenous or imported population, and the enduring 'colonial matrix of power' (coloniality) it leaves behind.
holes.why: Chapter 22 is entirely built on typologies of colonialism (settler, planter, extractive, postcolonial) and decolonization, which no existing taxonomy concept names—Fanon and Mills's racial contract cover pieces but not colonialism itself.

holes.name: Superiority Theory of Humor
holes.what: The theory—traced from Plato and Aristotle through Hobbes—that laughter arises from a felt sense of triumph or superiority over others, one of the three main currents in the philosophy of humor alongside incongruity and release.
holes.why: Chapter 19's philosophical spine is the superiority theory of humor as the basis of satire; the taxonomy has only Bergson's specific 'laughter' entry and no general concept for humor/superiority theory.
